newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf papers blame Netanyahu for Jerusalem attack.
newsitem.headline: Gulf papers blame Netanyahu for Jerusalem attack.

text.p: Gulf newspapers on Thursday heaped blame and scorn on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after a twin suicide bombing in Jerusalem which killed 15 people.

"Although only Palestinian militants were involved in this attack, this is a time when Palestinians living in the West Bank and Gaza are frustrated beyond endurance by the hardline policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu," the United Arab Emirates daily Gulf News said.
It joined many other papers in citing Israel's policy of expanding Jewish settlements as the root of the violence.

"There is no justification for yesterday's attacks, but (the) Israeli premier should blame himself first because his expansionist policies and anti-peace moves have created extremists among the young Palestinians," Qatar's Gulf Times said.

Qatar and Oman are the only two Gulf states which set up trade ties with Israel after it signed a peace deal with the Palestinians in 1993. But both have frozen the links following what they consider Netanyahu's hardline policies.
The UAE's Al-Khaleej daily said the attack might not be the last if current Israeli policies continued.
"It is Netanyahu who should be accused of what has happened in Jerusalem and of what could happen in other Palestinian cities under occupation," it said.
Iran's Akhbar newspaper said "Netanyahu should reap the grapes of wrath." The Islamic republic has virulently opposed the Middle East peace process since its inception.
Some papers said the United States, which has played a key role in the peace process, bore a serious responsibility in avoiding future attacks.

"The United States must adopt an even-handed approach to the peace process," the UAE's Gulf Today said. "Only then would it be possible to curb the despicable and cowardly terrorist acts which shed blood of innocents."
Some newspapers said Israeli and Palestinian leaders should seize the moment to give peace another chance, rather than let the attack destroy the prospects for peace.

"After yesterday's horrific bomb attacks in West Jerusalem, Benjamin Netanyahu and Yasser Arafat would need to summon uncommon determination and courage to give the peace process in the Middle East a new lease of life," Gulf Today said.
"The bombers must not win," said Qatar's The Peninsula.

"Nothing can justify the taking of innocent lives in such a terrible manner. The best way for both Palestinians and Israelis to achieve peace and security is for the peace process to move forward," it said.

Qatar, due to host a controversial Middle East and North Africa economic summit to be attended by Israel and Arab states in November, faces a possible boycott by many Arab states which have linked participation to advances in the peace process.
Some papers painted a bleaker picture, saying the peace process was already dead.

"Why shed false tears over peace and claim that the Jerusalem operation (the bombing) has put an end to it or delayed it? Where is peace? Who is murdering peace and mutilating its corpse?" the UAE's Al-Khaleej said.
"Let's stop manipulating and lying. A salute to the souls of the two Jerusalem martyrs and the souls of whoever died before them and whoever will follow them," it said.
